# Getting Water to the 30th Floor: How Municipal Pressure Works

Water doesn't need much help flowing downhill. The engineering challenge in a city water system is the opposite problem: lifting water hundreds of feet vertically, on demand, to faucets, showers, and fire sprinklers in tall buildings. Understanding how this works requires grasping one central concept—hydraulic head—and then seeing how cities manipulate it through elevation, pumps, and storage.

## The Physics Foundation: Head

Water pressure in a distribution system is usually measured in "feet of head." Every 2.31 feet of elevation gain costs you one pound per square inch (psi) of pressure. This works in both directions. If a water tank sits 150 feet above your kitchen sink, the water arrives at your faucet with roughly 65 psi of pressure—plenty for a satisfying shower. If your sink sits 150 feet *above* the tank, you'll get nothing at all; the water simply cannot climb higher than its source without help.
